prompt: In which situation does a request fail at once, with an error the app can show straight away?

choices.text: On a café's Wi-Fi that asks for a login first
choices.why: There the request does get an answer, from the café's page rather than your server.

choices.text: Inside a lift, with the phone still holding a connection to the mast
choices.why: That is the silent case: the request leaves and nothing answers.

choices.text: Airplane mode
choices.why: Right. There is no network at all, so the request fails in a millisecond.

choices.text: On mobile data with a small monthly allowance
choices.why: A metered network works; it costs money, it does not fail.

prompt: Android reports a network with the INTERNET capability and without VALIDATED. What is the likeliest explanation?

choices.text: A captive portal is waiting for the user to log in
choices.why: Right. The network is set up for the internet, but the probe did not get through.

choices.text: Your server is down
choices.why: The system's probe does not go to your server; it knows nothing about it.

choices.text: The phone is in airplane mode
choices.why: In airplane mode there is no network to report capabilities for.

choices.text: The network is metered
choices.why: Metered is a separate capability, NOT_METERED, and says nothing about reaching the internet.

prompt: NetInfo says isInternetReachable is true, and the planner's request to its own server still fails. How can both be right?

choices.text: They cannot; NetInfo has a bug
choices.why: Both can be right: the flag is about a different address.

choices.text: isInternetReachable only becomes accurate after the first request the app sends
choices.why: It comes from the library's own check, not from your requests.

choices.text: The phone switched to a metered network
choices.why: A metered network still reaches your server.

choices.text: The flag comes from a check against another address, not yours
choices.why: Right. By default NetInfo probes a Google address; your server can be down while it answers.

prompt: Which of these are good uses of the system's network state? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Waiting to send a request until a network exists
choices.why: Right. With no network at all, sending is pointless.

choices.text: Leaving a large download for an unmetered network
choices.why: Right. The cost to the user is exactly what the metered flag reports.

choices.text: Retrying a failed request when the network comes back
choices.why: Right. The change is a better moment than any timer.

choices.text: Deciding that the server is up, and skipping the timeout
choices.why: The network state says nothing about your server; only a request does.

prompt: Match each situation to what the app's request meets.

pairs.right: an answer from somebody else's page
an answer, at a cost to the user

right_distractors: a refusal from the operating system

prompt: What does the server's /hang path do with a request?

choices.text: Answers with an error after three seconds
choices.why: That would be a slow error; /hang never answers at all.

choices.text: Reads it, and never answers
choices.why: Right. The handler returns without writing, and the connection stays open.

choices.text: Closes the connection at once
choices.why: A closed connection is an error the client sees. /hang keeps it open.

choices.text: Crashes the server process
choices.why: The server keeps running and logs the request like any other.

prompt: curl asked /hang with --max-time 3 and stopped. What would the same command have done without --max-time?

choices.text: Stopped after 60 seconds, curl's default
choices.why: curl sets no limit on a whole transfer unless asked.

choices.text: Kept waiting
choices.why: Right. Nothing answers and nothing limits the wait.

choices.text: Printed the week, because /hang answers eventually
choices.why: /hang never writes an answer.

choices.text: Failed at once with a 503 status
choices.why: 503 is /flaky's answer, not /hang's.

prompt: Why does api.ts listen on 127.0.0.1?

choices.text: Port 8014 needs it
choices.why: Any port can listen on any address; the address decides who can connect.

choices.text: Node.js refuses any other address
choices.why: Node.js listens on any address it is given.

choices.text: It makes the server answer faster than a public address would
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; reach is.

choices.text: So that only your own computer reaches it
choices.why: Right. Another machine on your Wi-Fi gets no connection to it.

prompt: The status a server sends when it is temporarily unable to do the work, and which a client may try again, is ___.
A server sends one byte every fifty seconds. Which limit stops the request?

choices.text: A deadline on the whole request
choices.why: Right. It counts from the start, whatever arrives.

choices.text: A connect timeout of 10 seconds
choices.why: The connection opened long ago; that limit is over.

choices.text: A read timeout of 60 seconds
choices.why: Every byte restarts that clock, so it never reaches 60.

choices.text: None of them: a trickle is never stopped
choices.why: The whole-request deadline stops it.

prompt: Asked /hang with no limit of its own, after about how many seconds did Node.js's fetch give up?
fetchWeek printed AbortError rather than TimeoutError. What happened?

choices.text: The server refused the connection
choices.why: A refusal is a TypeError, fetch failed, with ECONNREFUSED.

choices.text: The network was too slow for the deadline
choices.why: That is the TimeoutError case.

choices.text: The app stopped the request itself, because the screen went away
choices.why: Right. The screen's AbortController was aborted; nobody is waiting for the result.

choices.text: The server answered 503
choices.why: That is an answer, and fetchWeek throws an ordinary Error for it.

prompt: A student starts uploading a 200 MB video of a lecture and watches its progress bar. Which limit fits that request best?

choices.text: A long deadline, with a read timeout that catches a stall
choices.why: Right. The judgement is about the screen: she can see progress, and a silence still needs catching.

choices.text: No limit at all, because she started it on purpose
choices.why: With no limit, a stalled upload spins for ever, the failure this lesson is about.

choices.text: The same five seconds the week screen uses
choices.why: Five seconds would cut almost any real upload of that size.

choices.text: Whatever the platform's default is
choices.why: Defaults differ, from 60 seconds to seven days; they are nobody's decision for this screen.

prompt: Put the stages of a request in order.
fetchWeek gets a 404. What does it do?

choices.text: Retries with backoff
choices.why: Only 500 and above are retried.

choices.text: Waits for the network to come back
choices.why: The network is fine: the server answered.

choices.text: Throws at once
choices.why: Right. A 404 will fail the same way however often it is asked.

choices.text: Returns an empty week
choices.why: An empty week would be a lie on the screen.

prompt: With a first wait of 500 ms that doubles after each failure, how many milliseconds does fetchWeek wait in total before its third attempt?
A request to add a 30-minute session times out. Why is sending it again not automatically safe?

choices.text: The server will refuse a second request from the same phone
choices.why: Nothing in the server refuses a repeat; that is exactly the problem.

choices.text: The server may have added it already and lost only the answer
choices.why: Right. A timeout says no answer came, not that nothing happened.

choices.text: A timeout means the session was rejected
choices.why: A rejection would be an answer; a timeout is the absence of one.

choices.text: Retries can be slower than the first attempt
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with whether repeating is safe.

prompt: Which request can be retried after a timeout without any key, and why?

choices.text: Paying for a subscription, because the gateway checks
choices.why: Without a key, nothing recognises the repeat; that is a second charge.

choices.text: Adding a session, because the student meant to add it
choices.why: She meant to add one, and a repeat adds two.

choices.text: None: every request that changes data needs a key
choices.why: Marking done changes data and is safe to repeat.

choices.text: Marking a session done: doing it twice leaves it done
choices.why: Right. The result is the same however many times it arrives.

prompt: A unique id the app makes up once for an operation, and sends with every attempt so the server can refuse a repeat, is an ___ key.
Why does a real client add jitter to its backoff?

choices.text: So the transcript output matches
choices.why: It is the reverse: jitter was left out so the output would match.

choices.text: To make each wait shorter than the last
choices.why: Backoff makes waits longer; jitter only spreads them.

choices.text: So phones that failed together do not come back together
choices.why: Right. A thousand identical schedules hit the server at the same instant.

choices.text: Because servers reject requests that arrive at round times
choices.why: No server does that.

prompt: The server is down and a copy of the week from this morning is saved. What should the week screen show?

choices.text: The copy, and how old it is
choices.why: Right. The age lets the student decide whether it is good enough.

choices.text: The copy, as if it were current
choices.why: That replaces 'I could not check' with a claim that it did.

choices.text: An empty week, until the server answers
choices.why: An empty week looks exactly like a week with nothing planned.

choices.text: A spinner, until the network comes back
choices.why: A spinner with no end is the first failure this lesson names.

prompt: screen.ts saved the week at 08:30 and was run again at 10:45 with the server stopped. How many minutes old did it say the copy was?
Where does the ECONNREFUSED behind 'could not reach the planner' belong?

choices.text: On the screen, so the student can search for it
choices.why: The student can act on 'try again', not on a socket error.

choices.text: Nowhere; it should be discarded
choices.why: Discarding it leaves the developer nothing to debug with.

choices.text: In week.json, beside the saved copy
choices.why: The saved copy holds the week and when it was fetched, nothing else.

choices.text: In a log, for the developer
choices.why: Right. The screen speaks the user's language; the log keeps the cause.

prompt: Match each state of the week screen to what it must show.

pairs.right: that it is asking, until the deadline
the week as the server sent it
the saved week and its age
what went wrong, and Try again

prompt: A student opens the week in a lift. The phone reports a validated network, the request leaves, and nothing comes back. With the code from this lesson, what does she see?

choices.text: A spinner that keeps going while the network still reports validated
choices.why: The network state does not decide the wait; the deadline does.

choices.text: After five seconds, the saved week with its age, and Try again
choices.why: Right. The deadline ends the wait, and the failure falls back to the copy.

choices.text: An error at once, because the lift has no signal
choices.why: A lift fails in silence, not at once; that is why the deadline exists.

choices.text: Three retries with backoff, then a blank screen
choices.why: screen.ts asks once, and never shows a blank screen.

prompt: Put what screen.ts does on a run where the server is down in order.
items: ask the server, with a five-second deadline
show the saved week with its age
